lesson.title: Racing the Fork: Why One New Strand Is Built Continuously and the Other Is Not
lesson.summary: Because DNA polymerase can only synthesize DNA in the 5' to 3' direction and the two strands of the double helix run antiparallel, one new strand is built continuously as the replication fork opens while the other must be built in short, separate pieces.
lesson.body:
As DNA replication proceeds, an enzyme called helicase unwinds the double helix at the site of replication, prying the two strands apart and creating a Y-shaped structure called the replication fork. This exposes two single template strands side by side, but because the original double helix is antiparallel, meaning its two strands run in opposite directions, one exposed template strand runs 3' to 5' toward the fork and the other runs 5' to 3' toward the fork.

This detail matters enormously because, as established in the DNA Polymerase chapter, DNA polymerase can only build a new strand in the 5' to 3' direction. For the template strand that is oriented 3' to 5' as the fork opens, DNA polymerase can simply follow the fork, adding nucleotides continuously to the new strand as more template becomes available. This new strand is called the leading strand, and it needs only a single primer to get started, after which synthesis proceeds smoothly and continuously in the same direction the fork is opening.

The other template strand is the problem. It is oriented 5' to 3' as the fork opens, which means that if DNA polymerase tried to follow the fork on this strand, it would have to build in the 3' to 5' direction, something it cannot do. Instead, the cell builds this new strand, called the lagging strand, in the only direction DNA polymerase allows: moving away from the fork. Every so often, as the fork opens further and exposes new template, a fresh primer is laid down near the fork and DNA polymerase extends it away from the fork until it bumps into the previous fragment. The result is that the lagging strand is synthesized discontinuously, as a series of separate short pieces rather than one smooth strand.

It can help to picture the replication fork moving to the right. On the leading strand, DNA polymerase simply chases the fork rightward, continuously adding nucleotides. On the lagging strand, DNA polymerase has to work in short bursts, each time starting near the fork and synthesizing back to the left, away from the fork, then stopping and waiting for the fork to open further before starting the next piece. These short pieces of the lagging strand are called Okazaki fragments, and how they are stitched into one continuous strand is the subject of the next chapter.
